paragraphs: He really was late. The others had waited for him, then decided to take the little flower-covered coffin to the church without him. It was poor little Ilusha’s coffin. The boy had died two days after Mitya was sentenced. At the gate of the house, Alyosha was met by shouting from Ilusha’s schoolmates. They had all been waiting impatiently, and they were glad he had finally come. About twelve of them stood there, each with a school-bag or satchel slung over his shoulder. “Father will cry, be with father,” Ilusha had told them as he lay dying, and the boys had not forgotten it. Kolya Krassotkin was at the head of them.

“I’m so glad you’ve come, Karamazov!” he cried, holding out his hand to Alyosha. “It’s awful in there. It’s really horrible to watch. Snegiryov isn’t drunk—we know for a fact he’s had nothing to drink today—but he acts as if he were ... I am always manly, but this is awful. Karamazov, if I’m not keeping you, may I ask one question before you go in?”
“What is it, Kolya?” said Alyosha.
“Is your brother innocent or guilty? Did he kill your father, or was it the valet? Whatever you say, I’ll take as the truth. I haven’t slept for four nights, thinking about it.”
“The valet killed him. My brother is innocent,” answered Alyosha.
“That’s what I said,” cried Smurov.
“So he will perish, an innocent victim!” exclaimed Kolya. “He is ruined, but he is happy! I could envy him!”
“What do you mean? How can you say that? Why?” cried Alyosha, surprised.
“Oh, if only I, too, could sacrifice myself for the truth some day!” said Kolya with enthusiasm.
“But not in such a cause, not with such disgrace and such horror!” said Alyosha.
“Of course ... I would like to die for all humanity. And as for disgrace, I don’t care about that—our names may perish. I respect your brother!”
“And so do I!” cried the boy who had once announced that he knew who founded Troy. It came suddenly and unexpectedly, and he turned red to the ears like a peony, just as he had that other time.

Alyosha went into the room. In a blue coffin edged with a white frill, Ilusha lay with his eyes closed and his hands folded. The thin little face had barely changed, and oddly, the body gave off no smell of decay. His expression was serious and, as it were, thoughtful. His hands, crossed on his chest, looked especially beautiful, as if they had been carved in marble. Flowers lay in them, and flowers covered the coffin inside and out. Lise Hohlakov had sent those early that morning. Katerina Ivanovna had sent some too, and as Alyosha opened the door, the captain was holding a bunch in his shaking hands and strewing them once more over his dear boy. He hardly glanced at Alyosha as he came in. He would look at no one, not even at his crazy, weeping wife, “mamma,” who kept trying to rise on her crippled legs to see her dead boy more closely. The boys had pushed Nina’s chair up beside the coffin. She sat with her head resting against it, and no doubt she was quietly weeping as well. Snegiryov’s face was eager, yet bewildered and exasperated. His gestures were wild, and so were the words that broke out of him. “Old man, dear old man!” he kept saying, gazing at Ilusha. While the boy was alive, he had always called him “old man,” out of affection.

“Father, give me a flower, too. Take that white one out of his hand and give it to me,” the crazy mother begged, whimpering. Maybe the little white rose in Ilusha’s hand had taken her fancy, or maybe she wanted one from his own hand as a keepsake. She fidgeted, reaching out for the flower.
“I won’t give it to anyone, I won’t give you anything,” Snegiryov cried heartlessly. “They’re his flowers, not yours! Everything is his, nothing is yours!”
“Father, give mother a flower!” said Nina, lifting her tear-wet face.

“I won’t give away anything, and to her least of all! She didn’t love Ilusha. She took his little cannon, and he gave it to her,” the captain said, and he broke into loud sobs, remembering how Ilusha had given up his cannon to his mother. The poor, crazy creature wept without a sound, hiding her face in her hands.
The father clearly would not leave the coffin, and it was time to take it out. So the boys stood close around it and began to lift.
“I won’t have him buried in the churchyard,” Snegiryov suddenly wailed. “I’ll bury him by the stone, our stone! Ilusha told me to. I won’t let them carry him out!”
For three days now he had been saying that he would bury the boy by the stone. But Alyosha, Krassotkin, the landlady, her sister and all the boys stepped in to stop him.

“What a notion, burying him by an unholy stone, as if he’d hanged himself!” the old landlady said sharply. “The ground in the churchyard has been blessed with the cross. He’ll be prayed for there. You can hear the singing in church, and the deacon reads so clearly, every word, that it’ll reach him each time as though it were read over his grave.”

At last the captain made a hopeless gesture, as if to say, “Take him where you want.” The boys lifted the coffin. As they passed the mother, though, they paused and lowered it so she could say good-by to Ilusha. For three days she had seen that precious little face only from far off. Now, seeing it close, she shook all over, and her gray head began to jerk wildly above the coffin.

“Mother, make the sign of the cross over him, bless him, kiss him,” Nina cried to her. But the head kept jerking like a machine’s. Her face twisted with bitter grief, and without a word she began beating her breast with her fist. They carried the coffin past her, and as it went by, Nina pressed her lips to her brother’s for the last time. On his way out of the house, Alyosha asked the landlady to look after the people left behind. She cut him off before he had finished.
“Of course I’ll stay with them. We’re Christians, too.” The old woman was crying as she said it.

The church was not far, no more than three hundred paces. The day was clear and still, with a light frost, and the church bells were still ringing. Snegiryov ran after the coffin, fussing and distraught, in his short old summer overcoat, bareheaded, his soft, battered, wide-brimmed hat in his hand. He seemed bewildered and anxious. At one moment he put out a hand to hold up the head of the coffin and only got in the bearers’ way. At the next he ran alongside, trying to find some place for himself. A flower dropped onto the snow, and he dashed to pick it up, as if everything in the world depended on that one lost flower.

“And the crust of bread, we forgot the crust!” he cried suddenly, in dismay. But the boys reminded him right away that he had already taken the crust and that it was in his pocket. He pulled it out at once and calmed down.

“Ilusha told me to, Ilusha did,” he explained quickly to Alyosha. “I was sitting by him one night when he suddenly said, ‘Father, when my grave is filled in, crumble a piece of bread on it, so the sparrows will come down. I’ll hear them, and it’ll cheer me up, not to be lying alone.’”
“That’s a good thing,” said Alyosha. “We should take some often.”
“Every day, every day!” said the captain quickly, seeming comforted by the thought.

At last they reached the church and set the coffin down in the middle. The boys formed a ring around it and stood reverently there through the whole service. It was an old church, rather poor, with many ikons that had lost their settings. But such churches are the best for praying in. During the mass Snegiryov became somewhat calmer, though now and then the same unconscious, and as it were incoherent, anxiety broke out again. Once he went up to the coffin to straighten the cover or the wreath. Another time a candle fell from its holder, and he rushed to put it back and spent a dreadfully long time fumbling with it. Then he sank back and stood quietly by the coffin, looking blankly uneasy and perplexed. After the Epistle he suddenly whispered to Alyosha, who stood beside him, that it had not been read properly, but he did not say what he meant. During the prayer “Like the Cherubim,” he joined in the singing but did not follow it to the end. He fell to his knees, pressed his forehead to the stone floor, and stayed that way a long time.

Then came the funeral service itself, and candles were handed round. The distracted father started fussing again, but the touching, solemn prayers for the dead moved him and woke his soul. He seemed suddenly to shrink into himself and burst into quick, short sobs. At first he tried to smother them, but in the end he sobbed out loud. When they began the farewells and went to close the coffin, he flung out his arms as if he would not let them cover Ilusha, and kissed his dead boy on the lips, greedily and again and again. They finally talked him into stepping back from the platform, but suddenly he put out his hand on impulse and snatched a few flowers from the coffin. He looked at them, and some new idea seemed to strike him, so that for a minute he apparently forgot his grief. Little by little he seemed to fall into a brooding state, and he did not resist when the coffin was lifted and taken to the grave. It was an expensive one, in the churchyard right next to the church; Katerina Ivanovna had paid for it. After the usual rites the grave-diggers lowered the coffin. Snegiryov, flowers in hand, leaned so far over the open grave that the boys seized his coat in alarm and pulled him back. He did not seem fully to understand what was going on. When they started to fill in the grave, he suddenly pointed in anxiety at the falling earth and tried to say something. No one could make out what he meant, and he broke off. Then someone reminded him that he must crumble the bread. He was terribly excited, grabbed the bread, and began tearing it up and throwing the pieces onto the grave.
“Come on, fly down, birds, fly down, sparrows!” he muttered anxiously.

One of the boys pointed out that it was awkward to crumble bread with flowers in his hands, and suggested he give them to someone to hold for a while. He refused. He seemed suddenly frightened for his flowers, as though people wanted to take them from him altogether. Then he looked at the grave and, as it were, made sure that everything had been done and the bread crumbled. Suddenly, to everyone’s surprise, he turned and started for home, even calmly. But his pace quickened more and more until he was almost running. The boys and Alyosha kept up with him.
“The flowers are for mamma, the flowers are for mamma! I was unkind to mamma,” he suddenly began crying out.

Someone shouted to him to put his hat on, since it was cold. He threw the hat into the snow, as if in anger, and kept saying, “I won’t have the hat, I won’t have the hat.” Smurov picked it up and carried it after him. All the boys were crying, Kolya and the boy who had found out about Troy most of all. Smurov, the captain’s hat in his hand, was crying bitterly too. Even so, as he ran, he managed to snatch up a piece of red brick that lay on the snowy path and hurl it at a flock of sparrows flying past. He missed them, of course, and ran on crying. Halfway home Snegiryov stopped short. He stood still for half a minute as if something had struck him, then turned back toward the church and ran for the deserted grave. But the boys caught up with him at once and grabbed him from every side. Then he dropped helplessly onto the snow as though he had been knocked down, and struggling, sobbing and wailing, he began to cry out, “Ilusha, old man, dear old man!” Alyosha and Kolya tried to get him to his feet, soothing and coaxing him.
